cohesive

/koh-HEE-siv/ — stress on HEE · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something cohesive holds together as a single, well-connected whole, with each part fitting logically with the others.

The debate team gave a cohesive presentation, each speaker building on the last.

Example

After weeks of rehearsal, the orchestra finally sounded cohesive — each instrument locked in with the others, no one rushing or dragging.

Cohere (to stick together) + -ive = having the quality of sticking together as one whole. The orchestra is cohesive because every part fits logically with the others; they form one unified sound. This is internal bonding, unlike adhesive (which sticks to other things).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

coherent: A coherent essay makes clear logical sense from one step to the next. Cohesive goes further: its parts do not just follow logically, they bond into one tight whole. A speech can be coherent yet still feel like separate points, while a cohesive one lands as a single piece.

integrated: Integrated means separate pieces have been combined so they work together, like two merged companies sharing one system. Cohesive is about internal bonding: the parts already belong to one thing and fit tightly together. Integration is the act of joining; cohesive describes how firmly the result holds.

congruent: Congruent means matching or in agreement, as when two plans are congruent because nothing in one clashes with the other. Cohesive asks for more than agreement: the parts must actively hold together and support one another as a whole. Congruent pieces merely fail to conflict; cohesive ones interlock.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

incoherent: disconnected, not holding together logically

fragmented: broken into separate scattered pieces

Where it sits · how tightly the parts hold together

linked → connected → unified → cohesive

linked vs. cohesive: 'Linked' means joined at a few points; cohesive means the parts hold together as one whole.

connected vs. cohesive: Connected ideas relate to each other, but a cohesive essay makes every part support a single whole.

unified vs. cohesive: A unified group agrees on a direction; a cohesive one is so tightly bound that nothing falls apart.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cohes-: shifted stem of cohere — from Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together' (past participle cohaesus) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive: having the quality or tendency of (Latin)

Put it together: Cohere swaps its -re ending for -s- (Latin cohaesus) before -ive: having the quality of sticking together — holding as one well-connected whole.

Use the root in a new word: cohesion: Weekly team dinners built the cohesion that carried the players through the playoffs.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Use cohesive when something forms a unified whole because its parts fit together logically or naturally — a cohesive team, essay, or argument. It suggests internal bonds, not just external combination. Avoid it for simple togetherness; save it for well-connected unity.
